platforms.title: 6 Early Dementia Signs That Aren't Just Getting Older
platforms.meta_description: Forgetting names now and then is normal. The NHS lists six early dementia signs that are different, plus what a GP checks and when a memory clinic comes in.
platforms.body_html:
You walk into a room and forget why. A neighbour's name sits on the tip of your tongue for a minute before it arrives. Past a certain age, moments like these start to feel loaded, and many people quietly wonder whether this is how dementia begins. The NHS is reassuring and firm at the same time. On its memory loss page it says most people forget things from time to time and that memory loss can just be a natural part of getting older. On its dementia pages it says something that sounds like the opposite but is not: dementia is not a natural part of ageing. The difference between those two statements is what this article is about.

6 Early Dementia Signs That Aren't Just Getting Older

The NHS describes dementia not as one disease but as a collection of symptoms that result from damage to the brain caused by different diseases, such as Alzheimer's. Which symptoms show up depends on which part of the brain is damaged. That is why dementia is rarely only about memory. Ordinary age-related forgetfulness, by contrast, does not come from that kind of damage, and the NHS notes it is often caused by things that can be treated.

The NHS lists these common early symptoms that may appear some time before a diagnosis of dementia:

  • memory loss
  • difficulty concentrating
  • finding it hard to carry out familiar daily tasks, such as getting confused over the correct change when shopping
  • struggling to follow a conversation or find the right word
  • being confused about time and place
  • mood changes

For Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia, the NHS adds a few more specific signs: regularly forgetting recent events, names and faces, asking questions repetitively, growing difficulty with tasks that need organisation and planning, becoming confused in unfamiliar environments, and difficulty with numbers or handling money in shops. Notice the words regularly and increasing. A single forgotten name is not the pattern; a steady drift is.

The Real Line Is Daily Life, Not the Odd Lapse

The NHS calls the earliest, mild stage of these symptoms mild cognitive impairment (MCI), because the symptoms are not severe enough to be diagnosed as dementia. In some people they stay the same and do not worsen; some people with MCI go on to develop dementia. The NHS also points out an awkward fact: you might not notice these symptoms in yourself, and family and friends may not notice or take them seriously for some time.

So the practical test is not whether you ever forget things. It is whether memory problems are starting to affect day-to-day life. The NHS advice on memory loss is short: see a GP if memory problems are affecting your day-to-day life. It is often nothing serious, it adds, but it is best to get checked because any treatment you need may work better if it is started early. It also warns against trying to self-diagnose the cause.

Book a GP Appointment and Bring Someone Along

At the appointment, a GP will ask about your symptoms and about everyday activities such as washing and dressing, cooking and shopping, and paying bills. If possible, someone who knows you well should come with you, so they can describe changes they have noticed and help you remember what was said.

The GP's first job is to look for other explanations. The NHS lists depression and anxiety, sudden confusion (delirium) caused by a condition such as an infection, an underactive thyroid, and side effects of some medicines as possible causes of memory problems. To rule these out, the GP will do a physical examination and may arrange a blood test and urine test, and you will be asked to do a memory or cognitive test. Stress and sleeping problems can also play a part.

If other causes have been ruled out, the GP may refer you to a specialist such as an old-age psychiatrist, a geriatrician or a neurologist, who may work in a memory clinic. The specialist may arrange a brain scan, such as a CT or MRI scan, and more detailed memory tests. The NHS notes that most cases of dementia can be diagnosed after these assessments.

Waiting is common. The NHS cites an Alzheimer's Society study showing that 1 in 4 people wait for 2 years before getting help for dementia symptoms, while an accurate and early diagnosis can have many benefits, including time to plan.

Here is one thing to do this week: write down three recent moments that worried you, with dates, and what happened next. If the list shows a pattern that is affecting daily life, take it to your GP and ask a relative to come too. This article is general information and does not replace advice from your GP.

Sources: NHS, "Memory loss (amnesia)" (page last reviewed 9 October 2023); NHS, "Symptoms of dementia" (last reviewed 10 July 2023); NHS, "How to get a dementia diagnosis" (last reviewed 17 July 2023).
